en: Sūtra: At that time, those celestial flowers arrived and immediately adhered, rather than falling away. Commentary: This section clarifies adhesion and non-adhesion.
There are two parts: first, it clarifies adhesion and non-adhesion; second, it clarifies that [the flowers] cannot depart.
This is the initial passage.
The Sūtra says: "At that time, the assembly of śrāvakas arrived, yet none were able to depart.
The Commentary states:
This clarifies that they could not go.
Sūtra: At that time, the goddess [appeared]. Why does it say "flowers"?
Commentary: The following is a question-and-answer refutation of attachments.
There are three parts:
first, the question of the goddess; second, the answer of Śāriputra; and third, the speech of the goddess.
This is the question of the goddess.
Sūtra: Śāriputra said, "I shall go because of this.
Commentary: This is Śāriputra’s reply.
Sūtra: The goddess said, "Cease; it is not at all in accordance with the Dharma.
Commentary: [The Buddha] addressed the goddess below.
There are two parts:
first, the brief indication; second, the detailed exposition.
This is the former.
Sūtra: "For what reason? Because [the person] themselves acts contrary to the Dharma.
Commentary: This explains the lower [category].
There are two [sections]:
first, the comparison between humans and flowers; second, the comparison between the Great and the Small.
Within the first section, there are two parts:
This consists of an initial manifestation followed by an explanation;
this is the manifestation.
The Sūtra states: "For what reason... up to... there is distinct conceptualization."
The commentary states:
This explains the reason for the distinction between humans and flowers.
"Non-conceptual" means the absence of conceptualization that grasps at a whole.
"Non-differentiation" means there is no distinction.
Furthermore, initially there is no common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), and subsequently there is no particular characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
Sūtra: "In well-expounded teachings, having reached this point, it is in accordance with the Dharma."
The commentary states:
The following section contrasts the "small" and the "great.
There are two parts:
The first part clarifies the distinctions among persons; the latter part clarifies the differences in the attachment to flowers.
This is the initial passage.
Regarding those who have gone forth within the Buddha’s precepts, there are two types of distinctions which are termed "unlawful," because they deviate from the true principle.
The absence of dualistic discrimination is called "acting in accordance with the Dharma," because it accords with correct principle.
The Sūtra says: "O Śāriputra, [from] 'only' up to 'and other discriminations.
The Commentary says:
The following clarifies that there are distinctions regarding attachment.
There are two parts:

first, clarifying that there are differences in discernment between having attachment and not having attachment; second, clarifying that there are differences in the severance of habituation between having attachment and not having attachment.
This section consists of two parts:

first, it clarifies the distinctions between having differentiation and having attachment versus non-attachment; second, it clarifies the distinctions between fearing and not fearing regarding having attachment versus non-attachment.
This is the initial passage.
Because the Bodhisattva is free from dualistic discrimination, the flower does not adhere;
because the Śrāvaka possesses dualistic discrimination, the flower adheres to his body.
Sūtra: "Only Śāriputra... up to "...could find no opportunity."
The commentary states:
The following clarifies the distinction between fearing and not fearing, as well as being attached and not being attached.
First is the analogy; second is the application.
This is a metaphor.
"Non-humans" refers to classes such as ghosts and spirits.
The sutra states: "If one fears birth and death, [these beings] will find no opportunity."
The commentary states:
This is a synthesis.
Those of the Two Vehicles fear birth and death; when various sensory objects find an opportunity, they disturb and delude their minds.
The Bodhisattva does not fear birth and death, and no sensory objects can disturb or delude his mind.
The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, Śāriputra, [it is] like a lotus flower that is not soiled.
The commentary states:
This clarifies that there is a distinction between habituation and abandonment, and between attachment and non-attachment.
"Habituation" refers to habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), which are precisely the state of heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Apart from their seeds, they possess a distinct substantial nature, such as the habituation of verbal abuse or the habituation of rising while dancing.
[Sūtra]: Śāriputra said: "How much time has passed since [the goddess] arrived at this place? [Commentary]:
The commentary states:
This is the second section from below, consisting of the dialogue between the goddess and Śāriputra, wherein she refutes the attachments of the śrāvakas.

The main text consists of five sections: first, an inquiry regarding the duration of her residence in the chamber; second, an inquiry as to which vehicle she has set out upon; third, an inquiry regarding the transformation of her female body; fourth, an inquiry as to where she will be reborn hereafter; and fifth, an inquiry concerning the timing of her realization of the fruit.
In the initial section of questions and answers, there are twelve in total.
This is the first question. The Sūtra states:
The goddess replied, “It reaches the liberation in which one dwells.
The commentary states:
These are the two answers.
Liberation is the unconditioned state of analytical cessation; it is the emptiness abiding in its own nature as nirvana with remainder; therefore, it is like abiding in liberation.
The Sūtra states: Śāriputra said, "Has it been for such a long time?"
The commentary states:
These are the three questions.
The Sūtra says: The goddess spoke again, up to the words, "How could it be otherwise than long?"
The commentary says:
This is a fourfold inquiry.
As for your liberation, how long or short has it been?
After some time, Śāriputra remained silent and did not answer.
[The Master] praised him, saying:
"This is the fifth instance of non-response."
The Sūtra says: The Venerable One remained silent and did not answer. Zàn says:
He was questioned six times.
Śāriputra’s discernment through wisdom is foremost; why does he not answer?
The Sūtra says: “Śāriputra said: ‘I do not know what to say at all.
The Commentary states:
This is the seventh answer.
Nirvāṇa is nameless, for its nature is beyond words; how much more so, then, could it have an inherent nature?
This answers the question regarding the duration of its abiding.
The Sūtra says: "That which reaches the heavens is called ultimate; all are marks of liberation.
The commentary states:
"These eight explain liberation."
There are three parts:
first, the heading; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion.
This is the heading.
Sūtra: "For what reason? Because it can be attained in the interim.
Commentary: The following provides the explanation.
There are two parts:
first, the explanation of the characteristic of liberation; second, the explanation of the characteristic of words and letters.
This explanation of the characteristic of liberation takes *tathatā* (suchness) as its essence.
The Sūtra says: "The same applies to the characters of the text; they can be apprehended up to the middle.
The Commentary states:
This explains the characteristics of the characters.
Within sounds, these are merely established through conventional designation; since there are no real characters, how could there be "internal" or "external"?
The Sūtra says: "Therefore, up to their nature being equal.
The Commentary states:
Because all phenomena and the nature of true suchness (tathatā) are, in their essence of true liberation, entirely without distinction.
As the Sūtra says: "Śāriputra, is it not said that [all things] ultimately constitute liberation?"
The commentary states:
This is the ninth question.
Śāriputra asks this because he takes the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) obtained through liberation from the fetters of afflictions as being itself liberation.
The Scripture says: "Heaven is called ultimate liberation.
The Commentary says:
This is the tenth explanation.

Those of the two vehicles are called those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) because, having not yet attained the fruit of Buddhahood, they claim it to be their foremost achievement and no longer seek it; they consider a meager attainment to be great, which is termed overweening pride.
All are of an unobscured nature.
For their sake, it is said that the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) obtained by being free from afflictions is called liberation.

As for those such as the Bodhisattvas who are called "those who have distanced themselves," for their sake, it is said that the true suchness (tathatā) which is the intrinsic nature of all afflictions is liberation.
Sūtra: Śāriputra spoke, saying, "The discernment of wisdom is such as this. Commentary:
This constitutes the eleventh question.
"What have you attained? What have you realized, that your wisdom and eloquence are such as this?
The Sūtra says: "The Deva replied, 'This is the height of overweening pride.
The Commentary says:
Eleventh answer:
All dharmas are fundamentally empty; there is neither attainment nor realization.
To speak of attainment and realization is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*), for while there is indeed a small attainment, it is not a great one.
Sūtra: Śāriputra said, "Up to what does one set out? Commentary:
This is the second question, asking: "In which vehicle (yāna) does one set out?"
There are four parts:
first, the question; second, the answer; third, the objection; and fourth, the resolution.
This is the initial question.
Sūtra: The goddess replied, [and so on] until "all have been inspired.
Commentary:
These are the two responses.
[Sūtra]: From the words of Śāriputra up to "he spoke thus.
[Commentary]:
This is the third objection.
The dharmas studied according to one's faculties are called "vehicles" (*yāna*).
To collectively lead toward the three vehicles while using terminology that is difficult to comprehend is called "profound intention" (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).
The Sūtra says: "I am the constant arrival; I am the Great Vehicle."
The commentary states:
There are three ways in which the fourfold penetration occurs.
First, he personally practices those deeds; second, he explains the Dharma accordingly; and finally, he resolves various doubts and difficulties.
This is the opening passage, which is absent from the older translations.
There are two kinds of śrāvakas:
First, the second chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* speaks of hearing the Dharma and receiving it with faith;
second, within the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" (*Śraddhāparivarta*), they are caused to hear by means of the Path.
Following the latter sense here, they are thus called "śrāvakas" (hearers).

Because they naturally awaken to the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and do not depend on the instruction of others, yet delight in solitary tranquility, they are called *pratyekabuddhas* (Solitary Realizers).
Furthermore, because their awakening arises through observation dependent upon conditions, they are also called *pratyayabuddhas* (Conditionally Awakened Ones).
Because it does not depart from compassion, it is the Mahāyāna.
The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, Śāriputra... up to 'I am the Mahāyāna.
The commentary states:
This corresponds to the Dharma proclaimed by that [Buddha];
it is propagated according to the capacities of sentient beings, or manifests in their respective forms; therefore, it is called the "Three Vehicles.
Sūtra: Furthermore, Śāriputra, [ranging] from grass and hemp to various fragrances...
The commentary states:
The following section resolves doubts and difficulties.
It refers to a doubt and difficulty raised as follows:
The celestial maiden manifests as those of the three vehicles; why then is it that in this room no followers of the two vehicles are seen, nor is the Dharma of the two vehicles heard?
The following four sections resolve these doubts and objections.

Although I possess the virtues of the three vehicles because I act for the sake of all three, my dwelling is exclusively that of the Mahāyāna; therefore, I do not see those of the two vehicles, nor do I hear the teachings of the two vehicles.

Within the following four sections, the first concerns exclusively Mahāyāna practice, the second exclusively Mahāyāna principle, the third exclusively Mahāyāna teaching, and the fourth exclusively Mahāyāna fruition.
Practice is like the fragrance of incense, for it increases what is wholesome;
principle is like the substance of the incense, for it can extinguish evil.
The remaining two [aspects] may be understood accordingly.
The initial text has three parts:
first, the metaphorical exposition; second, the doctrinal exposition; and third, the explanatory exposition.
This is the metaphor.
Campa (Jianbojia): formerly called Champaka; it does not exist in this land, and its fragrance is the foremost.
As the Sūtra says: "In response to such [questions], there are fragrances of ultimate merit," and so forth.
The commentary states:
This is the explanation of the Dharma.
According to the Sūtra, from "within this chamber" up to "because it is constantly perfumed."
The commentary states:
"The wondrous fragrance of merit is the practice of the Mahāyāna.
This concludes the sutra, from "Furthermore, Śāriputra" up to "the wondrous fragrance."
The commentary states:
These two are exclusively Mahāyāna principles.
*Nāga* means "dragon."
All were persons of great resolve in the Mahāyāna; upon hearing the principles explained, they understood those principles and returned home, carrying incense with them.
[The Sūtra continues: Furthermore, Śāriputra, [the discourse] proceeds to the corresponding dialogue.
The commentary states:
These three pertain exclusively to the Mahāyāna teachings.

The "twelve years" refers to the twelve stages (*vihāra*) of a bodhisattva: namely, the stage of spiritual lineage (*gotra*), the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā*), the stage of extreme joy (*pramuditā*), the stage of superior morality (*adhiśīla*), the stage of superior mind (*adhicitta*), the stage of superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā*), the stage of signlessness with effort (*animitta-sābhoga*), the stage of signlessness without effort (*animitta-anābhoga*), the stage of unimpeded understanding (*pratisaṃvid*), the stage of the supreme bodhisattva, and the stage of the Tathāgata.
The preceding twelve stages are called the Bodhisattva’s manifest entry into the Bodhisattva position.
Having never before heard the teachings of the Dharma of the Two Vehicles, and because the teachings and their principles accord with one another, they are termed "conformity" (*saṃprayukta*).
I have never heard a teaching on the principles of the two vehicles that accords with one another; I have heard only the teachings of the Dharma corresponding to the Mahāyāna.
Sūtra: Furthermore, Śāriputra, [you have heard] up to the most excellent Dharma.
The commentary states:
These four pertain exclusively to the Mahāyāna fruit.
By practicing the Mahāyāna, one attains these eight kinds of sublime fruits.
There are three parts:
first, the heading; second, the explanation; third, the conclusion.
This is the heading.
Sūtra: What are the eight?
Commentary: Explained below.
There are two parts:
first the question, and later the answer.
This is the question.
Sūtra: From "Śāriputra" up to "the most excellent Dharma.
Commentary:
The response consists of eight parts; the first is the aspiration.
Dwelling in an empty chamber, there are these eight rarities, signifying that abiding in true emptiness can give rise to these eight matters.
They may be fully understood according to their respective applications; fearing prolixity, I shall cease here.
Within lies wisdom, and without it evokes radiant light.

First, the primordial wisdom that universally illuminates the golden continuum of perfect realization is the light of day and night; it speaks only of the Mahāyāna, and does not rely on the sun and moon of the two vehicles for illumination.
Sūtra: Furthermore, Śāriputra, [he attains] the most excellent dharmas.
The commentary says:
"The two are rare."
With hearing the Dharma as a condition, afflictions do not cause harm.
Sūtra: Furthermore, Śāriputra... up to the most excellent Dharma.
Commentary:
Third is aspiration.
By drawing near to virtuous conditions, one thus gathers what is not in vain.
Sūtra: Furthermore, Śāriputra... to the most excellent Dharma.
The commentary states:
This is the fourth aspiration.
The Dharma teaching is profound and subtle; it proclaims the six perfections and turns the irreversible wheel of Dharma.
Sūtra: Furthermore, Śāriputra, [he attains] the most excellent dharmas.
The commentary says:
"The five rare things."
Because the requisites for offering are sublime, there is the joy of the Dharma.
Sūtra: "Furthermore, Śāriputra... up to the most excellent dharmas.
Commentary:
Sixth is the rare.
Regarding the four great treasuries (*mahānidhāna*): because his internal practice is perfected through immeasurable means of gathering [disciples], he externally manifests the four treasuries;
as his Dharma-wisdom is fully satisfied, he bestows abundant material wealth.
To have little wealth is called "greedy"; to have none at all is called "indigent.
To have no wife is called "widower" (gōn); to have no husband is called "widow" (guǎ).
To have no parents is called "orphan" (gū); to have no brothers is called "solitary" (dú).
One who is a traveler without kin is called "without reliance.
From the Sūtra: Furthermore, Śāriputra, [this leads] to the most excellent Dharma.
The commentary states:
This is the seventh rarity.
Internally one perceives the Dharma-body, and externally one beholds the Reward-Buddha; how much more so for the Transformation-Bodies that benefit sentient beings—what could they not achieve?
Therefore, if one prays with a sincere heart, they will appear in response to that thought.
Deeply moved and earnestly longing for the Dharma, he departed after having heard it.
This concludes the eleven Buddhas of the sutra.
Furthermore, Śāriputra attained the most excellent Dharma.
The commentary states:
This is the eighth rarity.
While the kalpas of sentient beings come to an end, the Pure Land remains eternally peaceful.
Whenever one beholds this small chamber, the Sage knows it to be a pure land; how much more so when he manifests transformations!

It is not that there are no celestial palaces, but rather that these external forms are adorned because his internal virtues are fully perfected. Even this small chamber is already rare and beyond comparison; a great kingdom as vast as the sands of the Ganges would be difficult to find even here.

He rescues from the eight difficulties, takes pity on the eight classes of beings, and severs the eight consciousnesses; he eliminates the eight perversions, manifests the Eightfold Noble Path, and attains the eight liberations—thus, what is rare and marvelous is manifested solely through these eight kinds.
Sūtra: “Is it only for Śāriputra, or even up to the dharmas of the Pratyekabuddhas? Commentary:
This is the third conclusion.
Therefore, no two vehicles appear; they hear only the Great Dharma.
[From the] Sūtra: At that time, Śāriputra transformed this female body.
The commentary states:
The third question below concerns the transformation of the female body;
it consists of three parts:
first, the transformation of the woman's body; second, the transformation of Śāriputra; and third, the restoration to their original forms.
The beginning consists of five parts:
first, the question; second, the answer; third, the counter-question; fourth, the provisional answer; and fifth, the definitive explanation.
This is the question.
Śāriputra, being of an inferior station, could not fathom the higher level; thinking she was truly a woman, he asked her to transform.
In the sutra, the goddess replies: "When it comes time for transformation, what would there be to transform?"
The commentary states:
This is the answer.
As for "twelve years," it may refer to the twelve links of dependent origination, expressed metaphorically as twelve years.
Because, while dwelling within birth and death, one seeks a real female body and utterly fails to find it.

Alternatively, it is said that among the twelve stages (*bhūmi*) of a Bodhisattva, the term "twelve years" is used figuratively; from the moment of first generating the resolve for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), one seeks a real woman and finds her completely unobtainable.
Some have personally attended Vimalakīrti and entered this room for twelve years; there is no need to speak of them.
Not only has he transformed himself into the form of a woman, but even the actual nature of a woman cannot be found.
Since there are no women, what could possibly be transformed?
Question:
As previously answered, one dwells here as if abiding in liberation, for a duration that is entirely without years or seasons.
Why is it now said to be twelve years? Answer:
Previously, the answer was given based on liberation through the true principle; therefore, the answer was that there is no fixed time.
Now, because this is based on the limits of practice and dwelling within the realm of birth and death, the answer given is twelve years;
thus, there is no contradiction.
The Sūtra asks: "Is it only Śāriputra who asks the correct question?"
The commentary states:
This is the third inquiry.
It reveals that she was already a woman, transformed rather than being truly so.
[Sūtra]: Śāriputra said: "What will be transformed? [Commentary]:
This is the fourth response.
Sūtra:
The goddess said, "It is so," up to the words, "I shall not turn back from my female body.
Commentary: It is said:
The fifth is the correct explanation:
all conditioned phenomena are like illusions and transformations; since a woman is not real, what is there to be transformed that could be made to transform?
The Sūtra says: "At that moment, the goddess did not change her female body."
The commentary says:
Regarding the second turning for Śāriputra,
there are three parts:
First, the turning question; second, the answer to the delusion; third, the formal explanation.
This is the turning question.
Turning back to inquire further, he again questions Śāriputra.
In the sutra, it is said that Śāriputra eventually took birth as a woman.
The commentary states:
"This answers the delusion."
Not knowing the cause for the male to cease and the female to transform, the Sūtra states:
“The goddess spoke again... [she] shall also be able to transform.
The Commentary says:
This is the formal explanation, which consists of three parts:
first, a brief illustration; second, a detailed establishment; and third, a citation of scriptural authority.
This is the first [section].
Sūtra: "As Śāriputra approached, she was in fact not a woman. Commentary: [It is said: "In fact, she was not a woman."
This refers to Guangcheng (Guṇabhadra).
By citing another to reveal his own case, it shows that the transformation into a woman was not real.
According to the Sūtra, the World-Honored One, based on this, stated that [the Buddha] is neither male nor female.
The commentary states:
This is an invocation of the teachings.
While appearances consist of male and female, in reality there are no males or females.
In terms of phenomena, there are male and female; yet in terms of principle, they truly do not exist.
Because the words are consistently [directed toward this truth], it is called "profound intention" (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).
Sūtra: "At that time, the goddess... where is she now?"
The commentary states:
"The three return to their original forms.
There are three [aspects]:
First, the manifestation of the inquiry; second, the response based on principle; third, the praise and citation of scripture.
This is the first [section].
Sūtra: Śāriputra said, "...up to: non-abiding and unchanging."
The commentary states:
This is a response based on principle.
Since the female form no longer exists, it is said that she is not there.
Since it was originally not a real woman, what is there to be transformed?
Furthermore, since the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is empty, what exists,
and what is there to be transformed?
The old [translation] says: "Neither existing nor non-existing. There is no real woman who existed in the past and does not exist now.
Since there is no real woman, where could she exist or not exist?
Sūtra: The Celestial One said, "The Venerable One is truly and authentically a Buddha.
Commentary: This praises and cites the teachings.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is fundamentally empty; where could it abide, and what could it change?
Furthermore, there are no such characteristics as those by which all phenomena are established; they are entirely non-abiding, for they arise anew at every moment.
Since there is no real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how can there be any transformation?
The older translation states: "All phenomena neither exist nor do not exist," because they lack a real nature.
[The] Sūtra says: At that time, Śāriputra, where will you be reborn?
The commentary says:
Fourth, the question of where one dies and is reborn.
There are four parts:
First the question, second the answer, third the objection, and fourth the resolution.
This is the question.

One does not ask from where [he comes], but asks only where he is going; since it has already been stated that "dwelling here is like dwelling in liberation," one does not inquire about the origin, but only about the destination.
Sūtra: The goddess replied, "Until I am born there.
Commentary: These are the two answers.
Regarding the place where the Buddha’s emanated person is to be born—indeed, they shall be born there.
Sūtra: Śāriputra spoke, reaching unto the place where he was to go.
Commentary:
This is the third difficulty.
Since transformation is not real, there is neither death nor birth; why then do you now say that there will be a place of birth?
The Sūtra says: The Deva said, "Venerable One, where will you be born?"
The commentary states:
Regarding the meaning of emptiness, within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), since all phenomena and sentient beings lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how could anything arise?
Regarding the meaning of conforming to reason:
Since the phenomena and sentient beings imagined by the pervasive conceptualization (parikalpita) have no substantial reality whatsoever, where could they possibly go?
How much less could there be birth for that which is a mere emanation of mine?
Thus, at that time, Śāriputra reached perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi).
The commentary states:
The fifth section below concerns the timing of the realization of the fruit.
There are nine questions; this is the first.
"How long will it be before you attain bodhi, and what will it be like?
The goddess replied, "It will be just as long as [the time it takes for] a sutra.
The commentary says:
This is also an answer.

Just as you have become a conventional person (pudgala) who is a worldling (pṛthagjana), so too will there arise within your body further worldling outflows (āsrava); after such a duration, you shall attain enlightenment (bodhi).
Sūtra: From the words of Śāriputra down to "the dharmas of ordinary beings.
Commentary:
This constitutes the third response.
In situations where it is unreasonable, even one’s status as an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is established once again.
The Sūtra says: “The Deva said, ‘Venerable One, until one attains the realization of Bodhi...
The Commentary says:
It is accomplished four times.
Since the principle of *tathatā* constitutes great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), there is no place of abiding, nor is there any time or stage at which it can be realized, nor any one who realizes it.
Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā* says: "In reality, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be named 'bodhi'.
The Sūtra states, from the words of Śāriputra: "...that which has already been realized and that which is yet to be realized.
[The author] comments:
Fifth, the refutation by citing scriptural authority:
"The present is directly realized, the future shall be realized, and the past has already been realized.
The Sūtra says: "The Venerable One has transcended the three periods of time."
The commentary states:
The sixth point concerns penetration through principle.

The Sūtra speaks of attaining bodhi throughout the three periods of time; this is said according to the conventions of worldly words and language. It does not mean that there are three periods of time within the ultimate reality of *tathatā*-bodhi such that one could speak of its realization, for *tathatā*-bodhi transcends the three periods of time.
Sūtra: "Furthermore, Śāriputra, [is it] up to the Arhat?
Commentary:
Seven further counter-questions.
In order to clarify the meaning, this question is posed.
The Sūtra says: “Śāriputra spoke... up to ‘attaining that which is non-attainment.
The Commentary states:
The eighth answer:
that which was never attained in the past but is realized now is liberation;
that which was thought to have been attained in the past but is found to be unattainable now is the realm of delusive objects.

When realizing the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), that which was previously unobtained is now obtained, while that which was previously obtained is now not obtained; therefore, it is called "attaining non-attainment.
Furthermore, it is said that non-attainment is itself attainment; if one wishes to attain, there is nothing to be attained and no attainment.
The Scripture says: "The Venerable One has attained realization, yet there is nothing realized.
The Commentary says:
These nine points establish the accomplishment.
Bodhi is likewise: that which was never realized from the beginning is now realized as True Suchness (*tathatā*).
As for "that which is not realized," it refers to that which was previously grasped as an object of realization; that which was [formerly] realized was perhaps a delusive realm.
Sūtra: After some time, Vimalakīrti attained the stage of non-retrogression.
Commentary:
This is the third section, the praise of Vimala.
First, her virtues are praised; subsequently, the reasons for her being born as a woman are explained.
This is the first [section].

Those born in the five states of immediate retribution are necessarily of extreme evil, frequently giving rise to anger, affliction, resentment, and poisonous intent.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The lion's roar is the definitive teaching that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
Second is the nature of having causes and conditions.
When bound by afflictions, it is called the "dharmatā-seed perfumed by extensive learning"; when free from bondage, it is called the "retribution body" (sambhogakāya).

The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The ālayavijñāna is called the empty tathāgatagarbha; because it is fully endowed with the perfuming of untainted dharmas, it is called the non-empty tathāgatagarbha."
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* relies on the meaning of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*): the afflictions (*kleśa*) are that which conceal, and the ultimate truth (*tattva*) is that which is concealed.

The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* relies on the meaning of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*): the ālayavijñāna is that which contains and conceals, and the seeds (*bīja*) are termed that which is contained and concealed.
The two kinds of that which can conceal and the two kinds of that which is concealed are both termed the *tathāgatagarbha*.
There are two types of outflowing [dharmas], both of which serve as dominant conditions (*adhipatipratyaya*):

The second category, "other unwholesome states," refers to those that are contrary by nature, as they oppose and obstruct the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas.
Because one attains *bodhi* through the severance of these,
and because these afflictions can obscure the true reality while their manifestation increases [the perception of] merit, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Because it possesses these two meanings, this unwholesome state is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Therefore, the teaching says:

Regarding the seven stations of consciousness (*sapta-vijñāna-sthiti*): the first is where the body is diverse and perceptions are diverse, such as humans, the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and those in the first dhyāna—excluding those at the beginning of a kalpa—possessing the perceptions of suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.

Second, there is diversity of body but unity of perception, as among the Brahmakāyika devas. This refers to those who first arose at the beginning of a kalpa; although their physical forms were distinct, they shared the same perception that the Great Brahmā was the father of all sentient beings.
In the third dhyāna, there is a diversity of bodies but a single perception, as in the second dhyāna, where the physical forms do not differ, yet pleasure and equanimity alternate.
In the fourth dhyāna, there is a single body and a single perception; that is, in the third dhyāna, there is only the perception of pleasure, and for this reason it is called "single-perception."
In the first dhyāna, because of defiled perception (saṃjñā), it is said that perception is one.
In the second dhyāna, because of two wholesome perceptions, perception is called diverse.
The third dhyāna is called "unity of perception" because of the perception resulting from maturation (*vipākaja-saṃjñā*).

Having already explained the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), the three lower formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) are established by their own distinct names; consisting of five aggregates or four aggregates as appropriate, these are called stations of consciousness.
